poiGPGP-desc:
Before the Great Mistake, the Great Pacific Garbage Patch was a warning that nobody heeded: a slow gyre of plastic turning in the middle of the North Pacific, thinly spread and mostly invisible. The Age of Plenty kept feeding it. When the Dark Age arrived, the factories stopped and the ships stayed in port, but the currents never did. Over the following century the debris kept gathering, bound together by nets, tangled hulls and drifting wreckage, until it became something no one had planned for: a floating landmass, hundreds of kilometres across.

No nation claims it, and no map agrees on its edges. It began as a refuge for people with nowhere else to go, the survivors of drowned coastal cities who found that a raft of compressed plastic would bear the weight of a shelter and a garden. Today it is a society of salvagers, rafters and ship-breakers, living on what the ocean delivers and selling what the mainland has forgotten how to make. The Patch's residents say it is the only land that grows when everything else is shrinking.

It is also a problem for everyone else. Its currents carry microplastics along every coast in the Pacific, the Müninstek lists it among the worst sources of Local Ecobalance Decay on Earth, and every government that has proposed clearing it has found the cost too high and the people on it too numerous to evict. The Patch does not need anyone's permission to exist. It only needs the sea to keep bringing it more.
GPGPpoi001-desc: The Patch is not solid ground. Its core is a dense mat of fused plastic, thick enough to build on, ringed by a looser belt of drifting wreckage that grows and tears with every storm. Settlements are anchored to the strongest sections and moved when the currents shift. Residents have learned to read the mat the way farmers read soil, and a person who steps on the wrong section can fall through.
GPGPpoi002-desc: The Patch's economy runs on salvage. Ship-breakers strip the abandoned hulls of the Dark Age, scavengers sift the mat for metals and old electronics, and the best finds are traded to coastal buyers who ask few questions. Its goods are cheap, its prices are fair, and its traders are known for never revealing where anything came from.
GPGPpoi003-desc: Several powers have a claim to the waters around the Patch, and none can enforce it. Its inhabitants answer to councils of rafts, family fleets and the occasional self-appointed captain. This has made it attractive to smugglers and refugees alike, and a source of constant worry to the governments of every Pacific coast, none of which can afford to ignore it or to go to war over it.
